newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac, Jospin face first test over stability pact.
newsitem.headline: Chirac, Jospin face first test over stability pact.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac and Prime Minister Lionel Jospin will face an early test of their power-sharing this month over France's approval of the European Union's controversial "stability pact".

EU heads of state are due to give formal approval to the pact, meant to limit budget deficits after the launch of a single currency, at a summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17. It is due to be adopted by finance ministers at a later meeting.
But Jospin, expected to attend the Amsterdam summit with Chirac, has said he does not feel bound by the pact, agreed in principle in Dublin last year, and wants it renegotiated.
An official in Chirac's office declined comment when asked whether the president could go ahead and give his approval without the support of the prime minister.

There is no precedent under "cohabitation" -- power-sharing between a president and government of different political parties -- for France going back on its word on an agreement made in international talks.

But analysts said the timing of the Amsterdam summit put Jospin in a tough position, leaving him a choice between backing down on a campaign pledge within weeks of taking office by allowing the pact to go through, or forcing a renegotiation.
"If they are serious about renegotiation they have to postpone the ratification of the pact," AMN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.
Approval could lead to a row with the Socialists' left-wing parliamentary allies, trade unions and the public -- all of whom are expecting a shift in Europe away from austerity.

But refusal to ratify the pact, seen by Bonn as a guarantee of fiscal discipline under monetary union essential to reassure German public opinion worried about the stability of the euro, could create a diplomatic crisis in Europe.
"I don't see how it would be possible to renegotiate something that has been negotiated by 15 countries," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said.
"The situtation is rather blocked. It depends on the strength of their (Socialist party) opinion and how much gambling they want to do," Brossard said.

The Socialist party is committed to launching a single currency but with conditions. It wants a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty, early membership for Italy and Spain, and a European economic government.
Apart from the stability pact, there is little significant difference between the Socialists and Chirac on EMU.
But Chirac, who pushed through a compromise with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on the stability pact last year, would be not be expected to go back on the agreement.

Analysts say they are still waiting until the new government is formed later week to see how many of the campaign pledges are translated into official policy and how far Jospin would go on Europe without risking the entire project.
A senior Socialist said on Tuesday however there was no doubt the new government would respect France's commitment to launch a single currency on time in 1999.
"Of course we must respect this deadline," Elisabeth Guigou, tipped to serve as European Affairs Minister in the new government, told RTL radio.
But in an interview with daily Le Monde published on May 20 -- before the left's surprising win in the first round of voting -- Jospin was unambigious in his opposition to the budget pact.

"The stability pact adds conditions which do not feature in the Maastricht treaty. The pact is a 'super Maastricht' of sorts and a concession which the French government made absurdly to the Germans or certain German circles," Jospin said. "Therefore I have no reason to feel committed to it."
